claims.text: The unusual stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is governed by residual stresses generated by thermal-expansion mismatch between a disordered BCC matrix and aging-induced coherent precipitates or compositional clusters.
A homogenized, non-aged HfNbTaTiZr alloy can provide a single-phase disordered BCC baseline with minimal precipitate content.
Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C produces coherent nanoscale precipitates or compositional clusters.
The aging-induced precipitates or clusters have coefficients of thermal expansion different from that of the BCC matrix.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between coherent precipitates and the matrix generates internal residual stress fields during processing and cooling.
The precipitate-associated residual stress fields impede dislocation motion and increase work hardening and microhardness after cold rolling.
Precipitate-associated internal prestress modifies the measured elastic constants and their temperature dependence.
Internal residual stresses alter high-temperature creep by changing the effective barriers for dislocation climb and glide.
Compared with a non-aged baseline, aged HfNbTaTiZr will have higher room-temperature microhardness.
The higher microhardness of the aged alloy will arise from dislocation pinning by residual stress fields.
Aging will measurably shift, and typically increase, the elastic moduli of HfNbTaTiZr over 293–1100 K.
Aging will reduce the tensile creep rate of HfNbTaTiZr at 1250 °C.
A rapidly quenched, non-aged HfNbTaTiZr baseline has minimal residual stress arising from matrix–precipitate thermal-expansion mismatch.
The proposed mechanism applies only while precipitate size, volume fraction, thermal-expansion mismatch, and coherency remain sufficient to sustain significant interface stresses.
Residual-stress and local-strain measurements can distinguish the aged state from the quenched baseline and test whether mechanical-response changes track the internal stress state.

Failure of precipitate-containing aged samples to show a significant internal-stress difference together with the predicted hardness, modulus, and creep changes would falsify the thermal-expansion-mismatch hypothesis.
